content_preview.title: Open Source Splits on AI Contributions: OpenJDK, GCC and COSMIC Restrict Them, Debian Allows Them, and the Linux Kernel Moves to Drop Its Tag
content_preview.summary: Open-source projects have adopted opposing rules for AI-generated contributions, from outright bans to disclosure-optional acceptance, while a Linux Foundation survey puts incoming low-quality AI pull requests at about 25%.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Background

Over the past several months, open-source projects that accept outside contributions have had to decide what to do about code written with large language models. The decisions have not converged. This analysis compares the rules several prominent projects have put in writing and the survey data that has appeared alongside them. Reported facts are set out first; the final section describes what the sources suggest the differences mean for developers.

editor_notes.content_quality: Genuine multi-project comparison (OpenJDK, GCC, COSMIC/GNOME, Debian, Linux kernel) plus survey data. About 1,320 words, inside the 800-2000 Analysis range. Reported facts come first under 'Current situation'; the 'Implications' section is explicitly labelled as analysis drawn from the sources, and 'What remains unclear' states open items. No prediction or opinion in the Herald's voice. Analysis requirements in config/editorial_policy.md met: examines a trend across several developments, not a single announcement.
editor_notes.source_verification: Independent-source count: 3 outlets, of which 2 are unambiguously independent of every project compared. (1) The Register (Liam Proven, 7 Oct 2026), independent journalism; (2) Phoronix, one outlet counted once although two articles are cited (GCC policy 29 Jul 2026; kernel Assisted-by 13 Oct 2026), independent; (3) Linux Foundation Research press release (20 Oct 2026), a research publisher independent of OpenJDK/GCC/COSMIC/Debian, but it is a press release, is Red Hat-sponsored (Red Hat is named in the article) and the LF hosts the kernel, so I count it as independent of the policies compared but only partly of the broader subject. Project primary sources: OpenJDK policy page and Debian vote page (2). Total 6 sources, at least 2 independent (Register, Phoronix): Analysis requirement (>=4 sources, >=2 independent) met. Snapshots read from disk: source-0 (openjdk.org/legal/ai), source-2 (debian.org/vote/2026/vote_002), source-3 (theregister.com COSMIC), source-5 (linuxfoundation.org press). The two Phoronix snapshots failed in chief:review (timeout 15000ms, file null); I live re-fetched both with curl (HTTP 200, full article text) and stored them as live-refetch-phoronix-*.html.gz in the sources folder (not listed in manifest.json); all Phoronix verification below is from those live copies. OPENJDK: policy title, date 9 April 2026, the 'must not include content generated, in part or in full...' sentence, private-use clause, three risks (reviewer burden, safety and security, IP), OCA ownership requirement, 'are trained on copyrighted and licensed content, and their output can include content that infringes those copyrights and licenses', the 100-lines/10-edited FAQ ('would still include, in part, AI-generated code'), 'reliably distinguishing human-generated content from AI-generated content is impossible' and the Skara checkbox: all verbatim/accurate. GCC (Phoronix; gcc.gnu.org not allowlisted and not cited): Steering Committee accepted the AI Policy Working Group's recommended policy, 29 July 2026; quoted 'legally insignificant ... clearly marked' and test-case exception sentences are verbatim (the article lowercases 'The' to 'the' mid-sentence, trivial); 'For the time being' and 'early 2027' revisit confirmed. Article does not state more than Phoronix reports, except marking scope (see corrections). COSMIC/GNOME (Register): COSMIC declaration quote verbatim; GNOME Calendar guide quote incl. [sic] verbatim; GNOME Extensions 'Extensions must not be AI-generated' and permitted AI learning aids/code completion confirmed; 'Debian decided to allow it, and of course, the kernel itself does too' verbatim. The Register gives no date for the COSMIC guideline change (see corrections). DEBIAN (vote_002): eight choices listed; Choice 5 'Responsible Use of Generative AI' is the Condorcet winner (281 quorum votes; beats Option 2 by 55); quotes 'neither endorses nor prohibits', 'does not diminish the contributor's responsibility', 'Blindly accepting or uploading AI-generated material without appropriate human review is inconsistent with Debian's established development practices', and 'but do not require them to do so' are verbatim (source typos 'enourage' elided correctly by the article's wording); mass bug filing/prior consensus/human oversight confirmed; Choice 1 (Social Contract, forbid LLM-assisted contributions) confirmed. The article states no vote date or counts. KERNEL (Phoronix 13 Oct 2026, headline 'Linux Kernel Developers Plan To Remove "Assisted-By" Tag Requirement'): it is a proposal, not a merge: a patch removing the documentation was posted to the mailing list, there was 'reportedly consensus' at the Maintainers Summit in Prague, views on LKML are mixed, 'would like the clarity'; Phoronix adds it 'will likely proceed'. The article body reports exactly this and its 'What remains unclear' says the sources do not state the change is merged. The title's 'Moves to Drop' is consistent with a posted removal patch and reported summit consensus, and is not an overstatement of a merged change. LINUX FOUNDATION: 59% (69% large projects), 25% PRs 'estimated to be low-quality ... AI slop' (31% large), 35% formal policy permitting GenAI, 32% no policy and no plans, 71% reduces barriers, 53% disagree improved trust, disclosure 'remains inconsistent', standardized attribution recommended, Red Hat sponsor: all accurate. The article does NOT repeat the 'maintainers estimate' framing: it says 'estimated' and, in the unclear section, 'survey estimates', consistent with the Herald's earlier clarification on the LF article. editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All policy claims about OpenJDK, GCC, COSMIC, GNOME, Debian and the kernel trace to the cited sources. Two imprecisions, handled by a corrections record: (a) 'In October, System76's COSMIC desktop added a similar rule': The Register (7 Oct 2026) says the guidelines 'have changed' but gives no date for the change; (b) the article says the limited LLM contributions GCC accepts 'must be clearly marked' (also 'clear marking of any accepted LLM contribution in GCC'), but per Phoronix only legally insignificant contributions must be clearly marked, and the test-case exception as quoted carries no marking condition. Consistent with Herald articles on Codeberg (2026-07/24), Debian (2026-07/26, which described four proposals; final ballot had eight, a later stage), OpenJDK (2026-09/11, same 9 April date and Governing Board approval), systemd (2026-09/09), GCC (2026-07/31), Torvalds LLM patch series (2026-10/17, which reports the kernel docs requiring Assisted-by tags) and the LF article (2026-10/21). Internal links use /article/<YYYY-MM>/<slug> and all four target files exist.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and descriptive. Implications section labelled as analysis; judgments such as 'least settled element' are grounded in the cited positions and not predictions.
editor_notes.originality: New angle: cross-project comparison with the Linux Foundation data and the kernel's reported move on attribution. Earlier Herald articles cover single projects; this one synthesizes them and adds the Oct 2026 developments (COSMIC, kernel tag, LF survey). Not a duplicate.
concerns: The two Phoronix articles are one outlet and the LF item is a sponsor-backed press release, so independence rests mainly on The Register and Phoronix.
COSMIC change timing ('In October') and GCC marking scope are slightly beyond what the sources say; covered by corrections.
Title wording 'Moves to Drop' refers to a proposed/reportedly agreed change that is not yet confirmed merged.
recommendations: State the date only when a source gives it; limit marking requirements to the scope the source states.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Qualifies as a genuine Analysis (6 sources, 2+ independent, 1,320 words, facts separated from labelled analysis). Substantively accurate with two minor recoverable imprecisions, published with a corrections note. Featured candidacy: 2 - open-source AI-contribution policy split across major projects is significant for a broad developer audience, though it is a synthesis of known decisions rather than new reporting
